docs.title: 3.18 Flexible Fluid-Structure Interaction
docs.text:
The coupled interactions between free-surface flows and flexible structures play an important role in a broad range of physical processes in both nature and industry. Therefore, DualSPHysics provides in-built capability for modelling flexible fluid-structure interactions. This capability is based on a unified framework, whereby both the fluid and structure phases are solved via SPH. Furthermore, well-known deficiencies with SPH-based structural modelling (linear inconsistency, tensile instability and rank deficiency) are addressed by adopting a Total Lagrangian formulation with kernel correction and zero-energy mode suppression. The fluid-structure coupling is handled via manipulation of the existing dynamic boundary condition within DualSPHysics, which does not require any geometrical knowledge of the interface. This, together with the unified SPH framework, permits straightforward implementation within DualSPHysics and retains its parallel scalability. A brief description of the approach is given below. However, for further details please see [O'Connor and Rogers, 2021].

Using the Cauchy momentum equation, as used in the fluid phase, to model the structural dynamics leads to serious issues with tensile instability. A solution to this is to reformulate the governing equations in a Total Lagrangian framework, whereby all relevant quantities and operators are measured with respect to an initial (material) reference frame [Belytschko et al., 2000]. docs.title: Smoothing Kernel
docs.text:
In SPH, any field variable at a location can be approximated by summing the contributions from neighboring particles weighted by a smoothing kernel function [@gomez2010state]. The kernel function \(W(\mathbf{r}, h)\) is defined such that:

$$ A_i = \sum_j \frac{m_j}{\rho_j} A_j W_{ij} $$ {#eq:kernel}

where:

  • \(A\) is any field variable
  • \(m_j\) is the mass of particle \(j\)
  • \(\rho_j\) is the density of particle \(j\)
  • \(W_{ij} = W(|\mathbf{r}_i - \mathbf{r}_j|, h)\) is the kernel function
  • \(h\) is the smoothing length

The kernel function satisfies the following properties:

Normalization: $$ \int W(\mathbf{r}, h) d\mathbf{r} = 1 $$

Delta function property: $$ \lim_{h \to 0} W(\mathbf{r}, h) = \delta(\mathbf{r}) $$

Compact support: $$ W(\mathbf{r}, h) = 0 \quad \text{for} \quad |\mathbf{r}| > \kappa h $$

where \(\kappa\) defines the support domain.

docs.title: Momentum Equation
docs.text:
The momentum equation in SPH form is derived from the Navier-Stokes equations [@dominguez2011neighbour]:

$$ \frac{d\mathbf{v}i}{dt} = -\sum_j m_j \left(\frac{P_i}{\rho_i^2} + \frac{P_j}{\rho_j^2} + \Pi $$ {#eq:momentum}}\right) \nabla_i W_{ij} + \mathbf{g

where:

  • \(\mathbf{v}_i\) is the velocity of particle \(i\)
  • \(P_i\) is the pressure
  • \(\Pi_{ij}\) is the artificial viscosity term
  • \(\mathbf{g}\) is the gravitational acceleration

docs.title: Artificial Viscosity
docs.text:
The artificial viscosity term \(\Pi_{ij}\) is introduced to handle shock waves and prevent particle penetration [@dalrymple2006numerical]:

$$ \Pi_{ij} = \begin{cases} \frac{-\alpha \bar{c}{ij} \mu}}{\bar{\rho{ij}} & \text{if } \mathbf{v} < 0 \ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} $$ {#eq:viscosity}} \cdot \mathbf{r}_{ij

where:

\[ \mu_{ij} = \frac{h \mathbf{v}_{ij} \cdot \mathbf{r}_{ij}}{|\mathbf{r}_{ij}|^2 + \eta^2} \]

with \(\alpha\) being a free parameter (typically 0.01), \(\bar{c}_{ij}\) the average speed of sound, and \(\eta^2 = 0.01h^2\).

docs.title: Continuity Equation
docs.text:
The density evolution is calculated using the continuity equation in SPH form [@crespo2008modeling]:

$$ \frac{d\rho_i}{dt} = \sum_j m_j \mathbf{v}{ij} \cdot \nabla_i W $$ {#eq:continuity}

where \(\mathbf{v}_{ij} = \mathbf{v}_i - \mathbf{v}_j\) is the relative velocity between particles \(i\) and \(j\).

docs.title: Equation of State
docs.text:
DualSPHysics uses a weakly compressible approach with the following equation of state [@gomez2012a]:

$$ P = B\left[\left(\frac{\rho}{\rho_0}\right)^\gamma - 1\right] $$ {#eq:eos}

where:

  • \(\rho_0\) is the reference density
  • \(\gamma = 7\) for water
  • \(B = \frac{c_0^2 \rho_0}{\gamma}\) with \(c_0\) being the speed of sound

The speed of sound is chosen such that density variations remain below 1%:

\[ c_0 \geq 10\sqrt{2gh_{max}} \]

where \(h_{max}\) is the maximum expected fluid depth.

docs.title: Cross-Referencing
docs.text:
You can reference equations like this:

  • As shown in Equation \eqref{eq:momentum}, the momentum equation includes pressure and viscosity terms.
  • The continuity equation (Eq. \ref{eq:continuity}) ensures mass conservation.
  • According to the equation of state \eqref{eq:eos}, pressure is related to density.

docs.title: Citing References
docs.text:
The SPH method was originally developed for astrophysical applications and has been extensively validated for free-surface flows [@gomez2010state]. The implementation in DualSPHysics follows the formulation described in [@gomez2012a] and [@gomez2012b], with specific optimizations for GPU computing [@dominguez2013a; @dominguez2013b].

For dam-break problems, the validation was performed by [@crespo2008modeling], while wave-structure interaction was studied by [@gomez2004using] and [@rogers2010simulation].

docs.title: Dambreak 3D
docs.text:
This example demonstrates a 3-D dambreak simulation with an obstacle. A rectangular water column is initially held at rest, then suddenly released at time \(t=0\). The water collapses under gravity, flows through a rectangular tank, and impacts a building structure positioned downstream. The simulation captures the complex fluid dynamics including wave breaking, splashing, and fluid-structure interaction.

For this dam break case, we use: - Fluid mk=0 for water particles - Boundary mk=0 for tank walls - Boundary mk=1 for building structure - Boundary mk=10 for a specific building wall (left side)

docs.title: Domain Setup
docs.text:
<definition dp="0.0085" units_comment="metres (m)"> 
    <pointmin x="-0.05" y="-0.05" z="-0.05" />
    <pointmax x="2" y="1" z="1" />
</definition>

Particle spacing (dp): The inter-particle distance is 0.0085 m (8.5 mm). This is the fundamental resolution of the simulation. Smaller spacing provides better resolution but dramatically increases particle count and computational cost.

Particle count estimation: For the water column (0.4 × 0.67 × 0.3 m), we get approximately (0.4/0.0085) × (0.67/0.0085) × (0.3/0.0085) ≈ 47 × 79 × 35 ≈ 130,000 fluid particles.

Domain boundaries: The computational domain extends slightly beyond the physical geometry (from -0.05 to +2 m in x, -0.05 to +1 m in y and z). This buffer zone allows for proper boundary particle placement and prevents particles from exiting the domain prematurely.

docs.title: Shape Mode
docs.text:
<setshapemode>dp | bound</setshapemode>
<setdrawmode mode="full" />

Shape mode: The dp option means particles are placed at the inter-particle distance dp. The bound option indicates that boundary particles follow the same spacing rules as fluid particles.

Draw mode: full mode creates complete solid or hollow objects with particles filling the entire volume or surface as specified.

docs.title: Fluid Block (Water Column)
docs.text:
<setmkfluid mk="0" />
<drawbox>
    <boxfill>solid</boxfill>
    <point x="0" y="0" z="0" />
    <size x="0.4" y="0.67" z="0.3" />
</drawbox>

Marker assignment: setmkfluid mk="0" designates all subsequent particles as fluid with marker 0. This allows the post-processing tools to identify and visualize water particles separately from boundaries.

Solid fill: The water column is completely filled with particles arranged in a regular lattice at spacing dp.

Position and size: The water column starts at the origin (0,0,0) and extends: - 0.4 m in the x-direction (length/downstream direction) - 0.67 m in the y-direction (width) - 0.3 m in the z-direction (height)

Aspect ratio: The water column is relatively wide (0.67 m) compared to its length (0.4 m), creating a 3D dam break scenario rather than a 2D one. The height-to-length ratio of 0.3/0.4 = 0.75 is typical for dam break benchmarks.

docs.title: Tank Boundaries
docs.text:
<setmkbound mk="0" />
<drawbox>
    <boxfill>bottom | left | right | front | back</boxfill>
    <point x="0" y="0" z="0" />
    <size x="1.6" y="0.67" z="0.4" />
</drawbox>
<shapeout file="Box"/>

Boundary marker: setmkbound mk="0" designates these as boundary (solid wall) particles with marker 0.

Selective filling: The boxfill parameter specifies which faces to create: - bottom: Floor of the tank (z=0 plane) - left/right: Side walls parallel to x-z plane (y=0 and y=0.67) - front/back: Side walls parallel to y-z plane (x=0 and x=1.6) - No top: Allows water to splash upward without ceiling obstruction

Tank dimensions: The tank extends 1.6 m in length (4× the water column length), providing sufficient space for the water to propagate and interact with the obstacle. The width matches the water column (0.67 m), creating a channel-like flow.

Shape export: shapeout file="Box" saves this geometry to a separate file for visualization and verification before running the simulation.

docs.title: Obstacle (Building)
docs.text: The building is created in three steps: void creation, external walls, and marker assignment for specific surfaces.

docs.title: Step 1: Create Void
docs.text:
<setmkvoid />
<drawbox>
    <boxfill>solid</boxfill>
    <point x="0.9" y="0.24" z="0" />
    <size x="0.12" y="0.12" z="0.45" />
</drawbox>

Void marker: setmkvoid removes any particles in this region. This creates the hollow interior of the building, ensuring no fluid or boundary particles exist inside.

Position: The building is placed at x=0.9 m, which is: - 2.25× the initial water column length downstream - Centered in the y-direction: y=0.24 m, which is (0.67-0.12)/2 ≈ 0.275 m from the left wall (approximately centered)

Building size: 0.12 m × 0.12 m × 0.45 m - Square footprint (0.12 × 0.12 m) - Height of 0.45 m, which is 1.5× the initial water height (0.3 m), ensuring the building protrudes above the water level

docs.title: Step 2: External Walls
docs.text:
<setmkbound mk="1" />
<drawbox>
    <boxfill>top | left | right | front | back</boxfill>
    <point x="0.9" y="0.24" z="0" />
    <size x="0.12" y="0.12" z="0.45" />
</drawbox>

Building marker: mk="1" distinguishes the building from the tank walls (mk="0"), allowing separate force calculations and analysis of building loads.

Wall surfaces: Creates boundary particles on five faces: - top: Roof of the building (z=0.45 plane) - left/right: Side walls parallel to x-z plane - front/back: Side walls parallel to y-z plane - No bottom: The building sits directly on the tank floor (which already has boundary particles from the tank definition)

Physical interpretation: This creates a hollow box structure that water will flow around and potentially overtop.

docs.title: Step 3: Special Marker for Impact Surface
docs.text:
<setmkbound mk="10" />
<drawbox>
    <boxfill>left</boxfill>
    <point x="0.9" y="0.24" z="0" />
    <size x="0.12" y="0.12" z="0.45" />
</drawbox>
<shapeout file="Building"/>

Impact surface marker: The left face (facing upstream, where water first impacts) is reassigned marker mk="10". This allows post-processing tools to specifically calculate impact forces, pressure distribution, and loads on this critical surface.

Why separate markers?: In experimental validations, pressure gauges are typically placed on the impact face. Using mk="10" allows direct comparison between simulation and experimental pressure measurements on this surface.

Shape export: Saves the building geometry separately for verification.

7.1.1 DAMBREAK

A 2-D dam break can be executed using wCaseDambreakVal2D_win64_GPU.bat (xCaseDambreakVal2D_linux64_GPU.sh in linux), which is the file that summarises the tasks to be carried out using the different codes in a given order:

Figure 7-2 shows different instants of the CaseDambreakVal2D simulation. The left frames show the PartFluid_xxxx.vtk (computed with PartVTK) and the right ones show the Slices_xxxx.vtk (obtained with IsoSurface)

Figure 7-2. Instants of the CaseDambreakVal2D simulation. Colour represents velocity of the particles.

With this example, the experimental data of [Koshizuka and Oka, 1996] can be numerically reproduced. The file EXP_X-DamTipPosition_Koshizula&Oka1996.txt includes the X-position of the tip of the dam for several instants (before the impact with the other wall).

Numerical gauges (<gauges>) allows the user to compute different magnitudes during the execution of DualSPHysics. In this case, two gauges were created at x=0.2 to compute the water column height evolution and at z=0.03 to compute the X-position of the tip of the dam. The gauges can be also observed in the right panel of Figure 7-2.

The 3-D test case consists of a dam-break flow impacting with a structure inside a numerical tank. No moving boundary particles are involved in this simulation and no movement is defined. This case is executed using wCaseDambreak_win64_GPU.bat (xCaseDambreak_linux64_GPU.sh in linux),

Different instants of the CaseDambreak simulation are shown in Figure 7-3 where the PartFluid_xxxx.vtk of the fluid particles, the CaseDambreak_Box_Dp.vtk and CaseDambreak_Building_Dp.vtk are depicted.

Figure 7-3. Instants of the CaseDambreak simulation visualized using Paraview. Colour represents velocity of the particles.

Using MeasureTool code, numerical velocities have been computed in the list of points described in the file CaseDambreak_PointsVelocity.txt, which are (0.754, 0.31, 0.02), (0.754, 0.31, 0.04) and (0.754, 0.31, 0.06) using information of fluid particles within the kernel interaction. Numerical values of Vx-velocity in the x-direction are shown in Figure 7-4 for these three points.

Figure 7-4. Numerical velocity computed at three different locations.

Pressure values are also computed using MeasureTool in the list of points described in the file CaseDambreak_PointsPressure.txt, which corresponds to locations in the front wall of the structure (Figure 7-5) using information of fluid particles within the kernel interaction. Due to the use of the dynamic boundaries, probes used for measuring quantities should not be placed at the exact position of boundary particles. The forces exerted by the boundary particles create a small gap between them and fluid particles (1.5 times h); as a result, probes placed inside the gap will have a reduced fluid particle population and will produce either an incorrect or no result. To avoid this issue, it is proposed that probes are placed at a distance 1.5h from the boundary positions.

In this example, the PointsPressure_Incorrect probes are placed at the exact position as the boundary particles at the building, while the PointsPressure_Correct probes are placed at a distance of 1.5_h_ (for the default conditions and parameters of the case) from the boundaries. The first probes produce no pressure results as the number of fluid particles for the interpolation is too small, while the second shows the pressure impact by the water flow.

Figure 7-5. Position of incorrect (red) and correct (green) pressure probes in CaseDambreak.

Note that the probes are not automatically associated with the smoothing length h and their position has to be changed manually if the resolution changes. Also, note that by increasing resolution (i.e. using a smaller “dp”) the gap is reduced.

Figure 7-6 shows the pressure computed at the correct numerical probes.

Figure 7-6. Pressure values computed at different locations in CaseDambreak.

This case also shows how to compute forces exerted against a structure. In this way the force is computed using ComputeForces as the summation of the acceleration values of the boundary particles that form the front wall of the structure (mk=21) multiplied by mass. Figure 7-7 shows the time series of the numerical force.

Figure 7-7. Force (X-component) exerted on the front wall of the structure in CaseDambreak.

In fact, the methodology outlined here was used in for the validation of DualSPHysics presented in [Crespo et al. (2011)].

Finally, an example to use FlowTool is also available in CaseDambreak. Two different domains are defined in the text file CaseDambreak_FileBoxes.txt. Figure 7-8 shows the red domain (RESERVOIR) where the water reservoir was initially created and the green box (TANK) to compute the flow rate in front of the obstacle. The output VTK files named Boxes_xxxx.vtk are also depicted in Figure 7-8 and the colour corresponds to the domain to which they belong.

Figure 7-8. Domains to compute flow in CaseDambreak; RESERVOIR (red) and TANK (green).

FlowTool also creates a CSV file, named ResultFlow.csv. Hence, figure 7-9 represents the outflow of the red domain and the inflow into the green one.

Figure 7-9. Outflow in the domain RESERVOIR and inflow in the domain TANK.

docs.title: Case Structure
docs.text:
The XML input file is organized into two main sections:

  • <casedef>: Defines the physical setup including fluid properties, domain geometry, and initial particle configuration

  • <geometry>: Specifies numerical methods, time integration parameters, and output settings

  • <floatings>: Specifies numerical methods, time integration parameters, and output settings

  • <normals>: Specifies numerical methods, time integration parameters, and output settings

  • <motion>: Specifies numerical methods, time integration parameters, and output settings

  • <normals>: Specifies numerical methods, time integration parameters, and output settings

  • <execution>: Specifies numerical methods, time integration parameters, and output settings

  • <special>: Specifies numerical methods, time integration parameters, and output settings
  • <parameters>: Specifies numerical methods, time integration parameters, and output settings
<constantsdef>                      
    <gravity x="0" y="0" z="-9.81" comment="Gravitational acceleration" units_comment="m/s^2" />
    <rhop0 value="1000" comment="Reference density of the fluid" units_comment="kg/m^3" />
    <rhopgradient value="2" comment="Initial density gradient 1:Rhop0, 2:Water column, 3:Max. water height (default=2)" />
    <hswl value="0" auto="true" comment="Maximum still water level to calculate speedofsound using coefsound" units_comment="metres (m)" />
    <gamma value="7" comment="Polytropic constant for water used in the state equation" />
    <speedsystem value="0" auto="true" comment="Maximum system speed (by default the dam-break propagation is used)" />
    <coefsound value="20" comment="Coefficient to multiply speedsystem" />
    <speedsound value="0" auto="true" comment="Speed of sound to use in the simulation (by default speedofsound=coefsound*speedsystem)" />
    <coefh value="1.0" comment="Coefficient to calculate the smoothing length (h=coefh*sqrt(3*dp^2) in 3D)" />      
    <_hdp value="2" comment="Alternative option to calculate the smoothing length (h=hdp*dp)" />
    <cflnumber value="0.2" comment="Coefficient to multiply dt" />          
</constantsdef>

docs.title: Constants Definition
docs.text: The <constantsdef> section establishes the fundamental physical properties and numerical coefficients that govern the simulation behavior.

docs.title: Fluid Properties
docs.text:
<gravity x="0" y="0" z="-9.81" comment="Gravitational acceleration" units_comment="m/s^2" />
<rhop0 value="1000" comment="Reference density of the fluid" units_comment="kg/m^3" />
<gamma value="7" comment="Polytropic constant for water used in the state equation" />

Gravity: Generally, it is used to simulate gravity's pull, and in this case it is set to -9.81 m/s² in the negative z-direction (Earth's gravitational acceleration) in SI. The \(x\) and \(y\) components are zero since gravity acts only vertically.

Reference density (rhop0): The reference density of the fluid being simulated. This value is used in the equation of state to relate pressure and density. All density calculations reference this baseline value.

Gamma: The polytropic constant (\(\gamma\)=7) used in the weakly compressible equation of state for water. This value provides a good balance between computational efficiency and physical accuracy for liquid flows.

docs.title: Density Initialization
docs.text:
<rhopgradient value="2" comment="Initial density gradient 1:Rhop0, 2:Water column, 3:Max. water height (default=2)" />

Density gradient mode: This parameter is used for the initialization of the density field for the fluid particles. Option 1 assigns \(\rho_0\) to all particles; Option 2 means the initial density distribution accounts for the hydrostatic pressure gradient in the water column, following the gravity direction, creating a physically realistic initial condition. This may help reduce initial transients when the simulation starts. Option 3 uses the max value of pressure according to the whole domain and the follows a global gradient rather than a local one. This option can be useful for floting body initialization.

docs.title: Speed of Sound Configuration
docs.text:
<hswl value="0" auto="true" comment="Maximum still water level to calculate speedofsound using coefsound" units_comment="metres (m)" />
<speedsystem value="0" auto="true" comment="Maximum system speed (by default the dam-break propagation is used)" />
<coefsound value="20" comment="Coefficient to multiply speedsystem" />
<speedsound value="0" auto="true" comment="Speed of sound to use in the simulation (by default speedofsound=coefsound*speedsystem)" />

Automatic speed of sound calculation: The speed of sound is automatically computed based on the maximum expected flow velocity. The auto="true" flag enables this automatic calculation.

Speed system: Represents the characteristic velocity scale of the problem. For dam breaks, this is typically estimated from Torricelli's formula: \(v = \sqrt{2gh}\), where \(h\) is the initial water height, taken as max position minus the min position of fluid particles.

Sound speed coefficient: The artificial speed of sound is usually set to 20 times the maximum system speed. This ensures that density fluctuations remain small (typically \(\leq\) 1%) while maintaining numerical stability. However, this definition may be case dependent. A higher coefficient makes the fluid less compressible but requires smaller time steps.

Note

Why artificial speed of sound?: Real water has a speed of sound around 1500 m/s, which would require mush smaller time steps. By using an artificially reduced speed of sound (typically 10-50 m/s for these flows), this approach allows maintaining weakly compressible behavior while making the simulation computationally feasible. However, this reduction applies only to scaled systems.

docs.title: Smoothing Length
docs.text:
<coefh value="1.0" comment="Coefficient to calculate the smoothing length (h=coefh*sqrt(3*dp^2) in 3D)" />      
<_hdp value="2" comment="Alternative option to calculate the smoothing length (h=hdp*dp)" />

Smoothing length coefficient: The smoothing length \(h\) determines the size of the interaction region between particles. With coefh=1.0, the smoothing length is calculated as \(h = \text{coefh}(1.0) × \sqrt{3dp^2}\) in 3D, which equals approximately \(1.73\cdot dp\).

Alternative formula: The commented _hdp parameter shows an alternative approach where \(h = 2\cdot dp\). The underscore prefix disables this option, so in this case the coefh formula is used instead.

Note

The smoothing length defines the "reach" of each particle's influence. Particles within a distance of \(2h\) from each other can interact. Larger \(h\) values create smoother fields but may over-diffuse sharp features.

docs.title: Time Step Control
docs.text:
<cflnumber value="0.2" comment="Coefficient to multiply dt" />

CFL number: The Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy (CFL) number of 0.20 is used to determine the integration time step. The actual time step is computed as \(dt = 0.2 \cdot h/c\), where \(c\) is the speed of sound. Lower CFL values ensure stability but increase computational time. A value of 0.20 is conservative and appropriate for violent flows like dam breaks.

docs.title: Marker Configuration
docs.text:
<mkconfig boundcount="230" fluidcount="9">
        <mkorientfluid mk="0" orient="Xyz" />
    </mkconfig>

Boundary markers: Up to 240 different boundary types can be defined (mk=0 to mk=239). This allows for tracking different wall sections, obstacles, or boundary conditions separately.

Fluid markers: Up to 9 different fluid types can be defined (mk=0 to mk=8). This is useful for multi-phase flows or tracking different fluid regions.

docs.title: Execution Parameters
docs.text: The <execution> section controls the numerical methods and simulation settings.

docs.title: Output Precision
docs.text:
<parameter key="SavePosDouble" value="0" comment="Saves particle position using double precision (default=0)" />

Single precision output: With value="0", particle positions are saved in single-precision (32-bit) format, reducing file sizes by ~50% compared to double precision. Internal calculations still use double precision for accuracy; this only affects output files.

When to use double precision: Use value="1" for cases requiring very precise particle tracking over long times or when post-processing requires high precision (e.g., computing derivatives).

docs.title: Time Integration
docs.text:
<parameter key="StepAlgorithm" value="1" comment="Step Algorithm 1:Verlet, 2:Symplectic (default=1)" />
<parameter key="VerletSteps" value="40" comment="Verlet only: Number of steps to apply Euler timestepping (default=40)" />

Verlet algorithm: Option 1 uses the velocity-Verlet scheme, which is second-order accurate in time and preserves energy well. It's the standard choice for SPH simulations.

Symplectic alternative: Option 2 is a symplectic integrator that may provide better long-term energy conservation but is rarely needed for short dam break simulations.

Euler initialization: The first 40 time steps use a simpler first-order Euler method. This "warm-up" period allows the particle configuration to settle from the idealized initial condition before switching to the more accurate Verlet scheme. This reduces initial numerical oscillations.

docs.title: Kernel Function
docs.text:
<parameter key="Kernel" value="1" comment="Interaction Kernel 1:Cubic Spline, 2:Wendland (default=2)" />

Cubic Spline kernel: Option 1 uses the standard cubic spline (M4 cubic) kernel function. This kernel has compact support (particles interact only within distance 2h) and provides good balance between smoothness and computational efficiency.

Wendland alternative: Option 2 provides a C² continuous kernel with better tensile stability properties but is slightly more computationally expensive.

Physical role: The kernel function W(r,h) acts as a weighting function, determining how much influence nearby particles have on each other. The cubic spline has a peak at r=0 and smoothly decreases to zero at r=2h.

docs.title: Viscosity Model
docs.text:
<parameter key="ViscoTreatment" value="1" comment="Viscosity formulation 1:Artificial, 2:Laminar+SPS, 3:Laminar (default=1)" />
<parameter key="Visco" value="0.1" comment="Viscosity value. Typically 0.01 for Artificial and 1e-6 m^2/s (water kinematic viscosity) for Laminar" />
<parameter key="ViscoBoundFactor" value="1" comment="Multiply viscosity value with boundary (default=1)" />

Artificial viscosity: Option 1 uses an artificial viscosity term with dimensionless coefficient α=0.1. This approach: - Provides numerical stability by damping high-frequency oscillations - Prevents particle penetration through boundaries - Is computationally efficient - Does not directly represent physical viscosity (water's kinematic viscosity is 10⁻⁶ m²/s)

Alternative formulations: - Option 2: Laminar viscosity plus Sub-Particle Scale (SPS) turbulence model for more physical representation - Option 3: Pure laminar viscosity for low-Reynolds flows

Viscosity at boundaries: ViscoBoundFactor="1" means boundary particles use the same viscosity coefficient as fluid particles. Setting this >1 can help prevent fluid particles from penetrating solid walls in violent flows.

Typical values: For artificial viscosity in dam breaks, α ranges from 0.01 (less dissipative) to 0.1 (more stable). The value 0.1 is conservative and appropriate for this violent flow case.

docs.title: Density Diffusion Term
docs.text:
<parameter key="DensityDT" value="2" comment="Density Diffusion Term 0:None, 1:Molteni, 2:Fourtakas, 3:Fourtakas(full) (default=0)" />
<parameter key="DensityDTvalue" value="0.1" comment="DDT value (default=0.1)" />

Fourtakas formulation: Option 2 implements the density diffusion term proposed by Fourtakas et al., which: - Reduces long-term density drift and accumulation errors - Smooths density fields without excessive dissipation - Improves pressure field quality, especially near boundaries - Is more computationally efficient than option 3 (full formulation)

Diffusion coefficient: δ=0.1 controls the strength of density diffusion. Higher values provide more aggressive density correction but may over-smooth the solution.

Why density diffusion is needed: SPH simulations can accumulate density errors over time due to particle disorder and boundary interactions. The density diffusion term acts as a corrective mechanism, nudging particle densities back toward their correct values.

Alternative options: - Option 0: No density diffusion (may lead to density fluctuations) - Option 1: Molteni formulation (older approach) - Option 3: Full Fourtakas formulation (more accurate but slower)

docs.title: Particle Shifting
docs.text:
<parameter key="Shifting" value="0" comment="Shifting mode 0:None, 1:Ignore bound, 2:Ignore fixed, 3:Full (default=0)" />
<parameter key="ShiftCoef" value="-2" comment="Coefficient for shifting computation (default=-2)" />
<parameter key="ShiftTFS" value="0" comment="Threshold to detect free surface. Typically 1.5 for 2D and 2.75 for 3D (default=0)" />

No shifting: With value="0", particles maintain their Lagrangian positions without artificial displacement. This is appropriate for violent flows like dam breaks where natural particle disorder is physical.

Shifting alternatives: - Options 1-3 activate particle shifting techniques that improve particle distribution and reduce void formation - Useful for low-Reynolds number flows or long-duration simulations - Can introduce non-physical effects in highly dynamic flows

Shift coefficient: The value -2 would be used if shifting were activated. Negative values indicate the shifting direction opposes concentration gradients.

Free surface detection: Would determine which particles are shifted if shifting were active. Not relevant here since shifting is disabled.

docs.title: Rigid Body Algorithm
docs.text:
<parameter key="RigidAlgorithm" value="1" comment="Rigid Algorithm 0:collision-free, 1:SPH, 2:DEM, 3:Chrono (default=1)" />
<parameter key="FtPause" value="0.0" comment="Time to freeze the floatings at simulation start (warmup) (default=0)" units_comment="seconds" />

SPH rigid body forces: Option 1 computes forces on rigid bodies (like the building) using standard SPH pressure and viscous force calculations. The building is treated as a fixed rigid body.

Alternative methods: - Option 0: No interaction (particles pass through) - Option 2: Discrete Element Method for contact mechanics - Option 3: Chrono physics engine for complex multi-body dynamics

No floating bodies: FtPause="0.0" is irrelevant here since the building is fixed, not floating. For floating objects, this parameter allows them to remain stationary during an initial warm-up period before dynamics begin.

docs.title: Time Step Calculation
docs.text:
<parameter key="CoefDtMin" value="0.05" comment="Coefficient to calculate minimum time step dtmin=coefdtmin*h/speedsound (default=0.05)" />
<parameter key="DtIni" value="0" comment="Initial time step. Use 0 to default use (default=h/speedsound)" units_comment="seconds" />
<parameter key="DtMin" value="0" comment="Minimum time step. Use 0 to default use (default=coefdtmin*h/speedsound)" units_comment="seconds" />
<parameter key="DtFixed" value="0" comment="Fixed Dt value. Use 0 to disable (default=disabled)" units_comment="seconds" />
<parameter key="DtAllParticles" value="0" comment="Velocity of particles used to calculate DT. 1:All, 0:Only fluid/floating (default=0)" />

Minimum time step coefficient: The minimum allowed time step is dt_min = 0.05 × h/c ≈ 0.05 × 0.0147m / 40m/s ≈ 1.8×10⁻⁵ s. This prevents the simulation from taking unreasonably small steps that would make it impractically slow.

Automatic initial time step: DtIni="0" means the code automatically selects the initial time step based on dt = CFL × h/c.

Automatic minimum time step: DtMin="0" uses the formula dt_min = 0.05 × h/c automatically.

Variable time stepping: DtFixed="0" enables adaptive time stepping. The code automatically adjusts dt each step based on: - Maximum particle velocity - Speed of sound - CFL condition - Force magnitudes

This is essential for dam breaks where velocities change dramatically over time.

Time step based on fluid only: DtAllParticles="0" means the time step is determined by fluid particle velocities only, not boundary particles (which are stationary). This is appropriate since boundaries don't move.

Typical time step evolution: In a dam break: - t=0: Small velocities → relatively large dt ≈ 10⁻⁴ s - t=0.1-0.5s: Peak velocities → minimum dt ≈ 10⁻⁵ s - t>1s: Flow slows → dt increases again

docs.title: Simulation Duration and Output
docs.text:
<parameter key="TimeMax" value="1.6" comment="Time of simulation" units_comment="seconds" />
<parameter key="TimeOut" value="0.01" comment="Time out data" units_comment="seconds" />

Output frequency: Data is saved every 0.01 seconds, producing 1.6/0.01 = 160 output files. This provides sufficient temporal resolution for accurate visualization and analysis without creating excessive file sizes.

docs.title: Particle Validity Checks
docs.text:
<parameter key="PartsOutMax" value="1" comment="%/100 of fluid particles allowed to be excluded from domain (default=1)" units_comment="decimal" />
<parameter key="RhopOutMin" value="700" comment="Minimum rhop valid (default=700)" units_comment="kg/m^3" />
<parameter key="RhopOutMax" value="1300" comment="Maximum rhop valid (default=1300)" units_comment="kg/m^3" />

Maximum particle loss: Up to 1% of fluid particles (value="1" means 100×1%=1% as a decimal fraction) can exit the domain or become invalid before the simulation terminates with an error. This tolerance accounts for spray particles and splashing.

Density validity range: Particles with density outside 700-1300 kg/m³ are considered invalid and removed. This represents: - Lower limit: 70% of reference density (indicates excessive expansion/void) - Upper limit: 130% of reference density (indicates excessive compression)

Why these limits?: In weakly compressible SPH, density variations should remain small (<10% ideally). The ±30% range provides tolerance for numerical oscillations while catching catastrophic errors like particle penetration or void formation.

What happens to invalid particles: They are removed from the simulation and counted toward the PartsOutMax limit. If this limit is exceeded, the simulation terminates early, indicating numerical instability or poor parameter choices.

docs.title: Simulation Domain
docs.text:
<simulationdomain comment="Defines domain of simulation">
    <posmin x="default" y="default" z="default" comment="e.g.: x=0.5, y=default-1, z=default-10%" />
    <posmax x="default" y="default" z="default + 50%" />
</simulationdomain>

Automatic domain sizing: x="default", y="default", z="default" means the simulation domain is automatically determined from the initial minimum and maximum particle positions.

Extended upper boundary: z="default + 50%" extends the upper boundary by 50% in the z-direction. If the initial maximum z-position, providing space for: - Water splashing above the building - Spray and droplet formation - Wave run-up on the building

Why extend only the top?: Water cannot splash downward through the floor or sideways through the walls, but vertical splashing is expected and needs accommodation.

Alternative specifications: You could manually set boundaries like x="0", y="0", z="-0.1" for posmin and x="2", y="1", z="1" for posmax to have full control over the computational domain.
